strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: the paper identifies why loss-based online data curation does not transfer to object detection (fragmented, architecture-dependent losses, proposal sampling/matching stochasticity) and proposes a principled, metric-aligned alternative that scores images by their marginal contribution to dataset-level AP.

The technical formulation is sound and carefully validated: the derivation of single-insertion ΔAP in the score-threshold domain (Eqs. 7–8, closed forms in Eq. 10) is verifiable, and the appendix provides both a full derivation and a Monte Carlo simulation (Fig. 5) confirming the analytic solution matches simulated marginal AP changes across detectors and priors.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: six representative detectors spanning one-stage, two-stage, and transformer families on COCO, with consistent gains (~+2 mAP on average, up to +2.7), ablations on teacher capacity, sampling ratio/overhead, prior choice, and detector families.

The synergy analysis (Table 2) is a notable finding: selection alone overfits (train AP +5.7, val -0.1) and strong augmentation alone is ineffective (+0.1), while their combination yields +2.5 val AP — the paper provides a convincing argument for why both are needed.

Strong evidence of robustness beyond the clean supervised setting: noisy-annotation sweep (Fig. 4), pseudo-label regime (Table 8), and comparison against eight alternative sampling metrics under a unified framework (Table 5), where DetGain is both more accurate and markedly more stable than loss/gradient/entropy baselines.

The method is genuinely plug-and-play (data-pipeline only, no architecture/loss/schedule changes), and the discussion of complementarity with KD methods (Table 6) is insightful — comparable performance to PKD/CrossKD without any loss or architectural modification, and further gains when combined.
weaknesses: The compute accounting is a material concern: DetGain incurs ~2.4–2.5× wall-clock training overhead (Table 4, Sec. 4.3), yet baselines are compared at equal iterations/schedules rather than equal compute. The convergence claim (Fig. 7, baseline needs 288k vs. 150k iterations) does not address that each DetGain iteration is substantially more expensive; a wall-clock- or GPU-hour-matched comparison against a longer-trained baseline is needed to substantiate the efficiency claim.

Evaluation is confined to COCO val2017. No second dataset (e.g., LVIS, OpenImages, Pascal VOC) or alternative annotation protocol is tested, leaving generalization of the claimed architecture-agnostic, dataset-level behavior unverified outside a single benchmark. Results are also single-run with no variance/significance reporting, despite gains of 1.6–3.0 mAP where run-to-run variance matters.

The reported gains conflate two components (strong augmentation + DetGain sampling); while Table 2 disentangles them, the augmentation pipeline itself (Table 10) is heavily tuned per detector family (branch probabilities, strengths, per-model Copy-Paste rates), raising the question of how much of the improvement stems from this bespoke augmentation configuration versus the curation mechanism itself.

The uniform-prior + fixed global T:F=1:9 simplification makes the absolute DetGain values crude proxies for true marginal AP; the empirical defense (Table 11, ranking robustness) is adequate but the theoretical gap between the estimated quantity and the actual δmAP definition (Eq. 2) — including the first-order additivity assumption and ignoring within-batch interactions among multiple insertions of the same class — is not quantified beyond O(|B|/|D|).

Some claims are overstated or under-specified: the 'first' online curation pipeline for detection sits in tension with [61] (which the paper acknowledges); the pseudo-labeling experiment uses a YOLOv8-nano generator whose interaction with the scoring teacher is only briefly motivated; and no code release or reproducibility statement is evident, despite heavy dependence on unspecified augmentation strengths/probabilities.

Several presentation-level issues: Eq. (7)'s treatment ignores precision effects on FP-dominated regions of the PR curve as stated but the implications for ranking among images with many FPs are not analyzed; Table 3 numbers for ATSS/VFNet baselines appear inconsistent with Table 1 (39.4/40.7 vs. matching values only in one table), which could confuse readers; and the small k=10% regime's non-monotonicity (39.6 vs. 39.9 at 20%) is explained only heuristically.

strengths: The paper targets a genuinely underexplored problem—online data curation for object detection—and the proposed metric-aware signal (marginal contribution to dataset-level AP) is a sensible, well-motivated alternative to unstable loss-based learnability scores in detection.

The technical derivation is careful: the single-insertion ΔAP analysis (Eqs. 7–8, Appendix A3) is correct, and the closed forms under a uniform Beta(1,1) prior (Eqs. 25–26) are validated by Monte Carlo simulation (Appendix 4, Fig. 5), which supports the correctness of the estimator.

The empirical evaluation is broad: six representative detectors spanning one-stage, two-stage, and transformer architectures (Table 1), comparisons against seven alternative sampling metrics under a unified framework (Table 5), ablations on teacher capacity, sampling ratio, noise robustness, pseudo-labels, prior choice, and augmentation schedules (Tables 2–4, 7, 8, 10, 11).

The method is genuinely plug-and-play at the data-pipeline level (Algorithm 1, Listing 1), and implementation details (super-batch size, selection ratio, augmentation probabilities per detector family) are reported at a level that supports reproducibility.
The robustness results under annotation noise (Fig. 4) and pseudo-labeled data (Table 8), and the complementarity with KD methods (Table 6), add practical value beyond the headline accuracy numbers.
weaknesses: The compute-fairness of the comparison is not established. DetGain adds ~2.5× wall-clock training overhead (Sec. 4.3) and additionally requires a large pretrained teacher (ResNet-101/152) trained on the same dataset. The reported +1.6 to +2.7 mAP gains are not compared against a baseline trained with an equivalent compute budget (e.g., 2.5× schedule or stronger augmentation for the same wall-clock). Figure 7 actually undercuts the efficiency claim: Deformable DETR needs 150K vs. 288K iterations (~2× fewer) but each iteration costs ~2.4× more, implying roughly parity or worse in wall-clock time, not a saving.

The framing overstates novelty. The core recipe—teacher–student gap scoring with strong augmentation—is directly inherited from RHO-LOSS/JEST/ACED; the contribution is essentially substituting the loss gap with an AP-based gap (and generalizing the offline image-AP metric of [61] to an online setting). The delta over [61] and RHO-LOSS is real but incremental, and the paper leans heavily on the teacher, making it partially an implicit-KD method (as the authors themselves note in Sec. 4.3).

Key details of the online estimator are underspecified. The dataset-level counts (T_c,τ, F_c,τ, T^GT_c) are central to Eqs. (9)–(10), yet the paper does not explain how T and F evolve during training as the student changes, whether they are computed from teacher predictions, or how stale counts affect the score; the fixed T:F = 1:9 simplification (Appendix A3.4) further suggests the score may be less dynamic than claimed.

The uniform-prior assumption is convenient but weakly justified: under Beta(1,1) the 'global' TP/FP distributions are identical for teacher and student, so the ranking signal comes mainly from the monotone rescaling of scores and the 1/T^GT_c class weighting rather than from a genuine model of either model's score distribution. The Beta-fit ablation (Table 11) shows near-identical results, which raises the question of how much of the method's behavior is captured by a much simpler score heuristic (e.g., a function of max score × IoU per image).

Evaluation is limited to a single benchmark (COCO val2017). No second dataset (VOC, LVIS, Objects365) is provided, and results appear to be single runs without variance estimates, which matters given that several reported differences (e.g., 39.6 vs. 39.9 across teacher backbones in Table 3) are small.

Some ablation interactions muddy attribution: Table 2 shows DetGain sampling alone slightly hurts validation AP (37.3 vs. 37.4), and the headline gains only materialize when combined with the strong augmentation stack (Table 10) whose probabilities are hand-tuned per detector family—so it is unclear how much of the improvement is the augmentation pipeline versus the curation signal itself.

Presentation issues: 'Xinyue et al. [18]' cites a first name; the appendix references are inconsistent (main text cites 'Appendix 6' for the prior ablation while Fig. 2C points elsewhere; supplementary figure/appendix numbering is misaligned); the YOLOv8 citation [50] points to an inappropriate venue; several small grammatical errors (e.g., 'KD methods... introduces' in Sec. 4.5).

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and original: adapting online data curation (RHO-LOSS/JEST-style teacher-student learnability) to object detection by replacing unstable loss-based signals with a score aligned to dataset-level mAP. The identification of why loss-based learnability breaks for detection (fragmented multi-task losses, stochastic proposal/matching dynamics) is convincing and clearly articulated.

The technical formulation is solid: the derivation of single-insertion ΔAP in the score-threshold domain (Eqs. 7-8), the closed forms under a uniform prior (Eqs. 25-26), and the Monte Carlo verification (Appendix 4, Fig. 5) together provide credible evidence that the estimator is mathematically correct and numerically stable. The O(1) per-detection cost makes online use plausible.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for this problem: six representative detectors spanning one-stage, two-stage, and transformer families (Table 1) with consistent ~+2 mAP gains; a broad comparison against seven alternative sampling metrics under a unified online framework (Table 5); ablations on teacher backbone, sampling ratio, augmentation interplay (Table 2), uniform vs. model-specific priors (Table 11), and asynchronous teacher architectures (Table 7); plus robustness under synthetic annotation noise (Fig. 4) and pseudo-labels (Table 8).

The combination of strong online augmentation with DetGain-based subsampling is a sensible and well-analyzed design choice: the overfitting of pure learnability sampling (Table 2) is honestly reported and the augmentation-curation complementarity is convincingly demonstrated.

The method is genuinely non-intrusive (data-pipeline only, Algorithm 1 and Listing 1 are clear), which supports the plug-and-play claim, and the discussion with KD methods (Table 6) adds useful context showing complementarity rather than replacement.
weaknesses: The training cost is substantial and the efficiency claims are somewhat overstated. Table 4 reports ×2.4 wall-clock at the default 20% sampling ratio (and ×2.5 in the text). Figure 7 shows Deformable DETR reaches baseline performance in ~52% of iterations, but with ~2.4× per-iteration cost this is roughly break-even or worse in wall-clock terms. The paper frames the overhead as an 'offline investment,' which is fair, but the abstract/intro claims of improved 'efficiency (convergence speed)' should be more carefully qualified.

The comparison to the baseline in Table 1 may not fully isolate the contribution of curation: the teacher (Res101/Res152 pretrained on the same training set) is an additional resource the baseline does not have, and a Res152 Faster R-CNN trained directly likely exceeds the student+DetGain result (~40.0 AP). The method's value proposition (a cheaper student matching a larger model) is plausible for inference-constrained deployment, but the paper does not explicitly discuss this teacher-vs-student trade-off, and Table 6 (where a same-architecture Res50 teacher still yields +2.3) only partially addresses it.

Evaluation is limited to COCO 2017. Given the claim of a general data-efficient curation strategy, at least one additional benchmark (e.g., LVIS, Objects365, or a long-tail setting) would materially strengthen the generality claims, especially since the method is claimed to naturally mitigate long-tail imbalance via the 1/T_c^GT normalization.

Some experimental details are inconsistent or under-specified: Table 1 describes an 80-image super-batch while Table 5 uses 64; augmentation probabilities are 'roughly adjusted per detector family' (Appendix 5), which introduces per-method tuning that is hard to audit; no code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of a method with many pipeline-level choices.

The first-order additive approximation (Eq. 9, Appendix A3.4) treats an image's multiple detections as independent insertions and ignores intra-image interaction effects; while the ordering-robustness argument is plausible and Monte Carlo validates the single-insertion case, there is no direct empirical validation of the image-level aggregation against exact marginal mAP computation.

Minor presentation issues: the derivation relies on a non-interpolated AP definition that differs from COCO's 101-point interpolation; several claims (e.g., 'first data-efficient online curation pipeline' in the conclusion) are strong given related metric-driven selection work [61]; the'+Data Aug.' column interactions would benefit from statistical significance reporting given gains of +0.1-0.8 in some cells.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper identifies a genuine gap—online data curation for object detection—and proposes a principled selection criterion (marginal contribution to dataset-level AP) that is architecture-agnostic and decoupled from detector internals, addressing a real weakness of loss-based learnability signals in detection (fragmented multi-task losses, proposal sampling stochasticity).

Technically sound derivation: the marginal ΔAP analysis (Eqs. 4-10) is clearly developed, and the closed-form estimators under a uniform Beta(1,1) prior are verified both by Monte Carlo simulation (Appendix 4, Fig. 7 shows excellent agreement) and by validating the first-order additivity assumption with ranking-stability experiments (Fig. 6, Spearman ρ≈1 for realistic batch sizes).

Comprehensive and well-designed experiments: six diverse detectors (2-stage, 1-stage anchor-based/anchor-free, transformer) on COCO with 3 seeds and std reported; consistent ~+2 mAP gains; ablations on teacher capacity, augmentation/sampling interplay (Table 2), and comparison against multiple alternative sampling metrics (Table 4) where DetGain outperforms loss-learnability, GradNorm, entropy, and image-AP baselines.

Strong robustness analysis: controlled noise injection (Fig. 5), pseudo-label experiments (Table 7), asynchronous teacher ablations (Table 6), additional datasets (VOC, BDD100K), and longer-schedule experiments (Table 13) that convincingly rule out the 'it just trains longer' objection—baseline overfits at 3x while DetGain keeps improving.

Honest treatment of limitations: the paper explicitly reports the substantial runtime overhead (+200% wall-clock, Table 12), proposes a dynamic selection-ratio schedule that retains 98.8% of performance at ~30% less overhead, and demonstrates convergence speedup (Fig. 9: baseline performance reached in ~52% of iterations). The limitations section is candid.
weaknesses: Computational cost is significant: per-iteration time triples (0.25s → 0.75s) due to the extra no-grad scoring pass over a larger super-batch and stronger augmentation I/O. While convergence-speedup and the dynamic-ratio schedule mitigate this, the 'data-efficient' framing is weakened; a wall-clock-matched comparison against a longer-trained baseline would strengthen the efficiency claim.

Entanglement between DetGain and the strong augmentation pipeline: Table 2 shows augmentation alone yields almost nothing (+0.1) and sampling alone overfits; the headline gains depend on the specific pairing. The paper argues this is a contribution (complementarity), but it makes it harder to isolate how much of the benefit comes from the augmentation recipe itself versus the DetGain ranking, and the augmentation probabilities are hand-tuned per detector family (Table 9), which reduces plug-and-play appeal.

The method requires a pretrained teacher trained on the same dataset with a stronger backbone (Res152/Res101), which is an additional training cost and makes the setup close to implicit KD; the comparison to explicit KD methods (Table 5) is helpful, but a comparison against simply training longer with the same total compute budget (including teacher training) is not provided.

Absolute DetGain magnitudes are tiny (per-detection ΔAP on the order of 1e-3 to 1e-5), so selection rests entirely on the relative ordering under a first-order additive approximation with a uniform score prior; the empirical justification (Figs. 4, 6, 10) is good but the reliance on rank stability rather than accurate value estimation deserves more discussion of failure regimes (e.g., very small datasets or highly non-uniform score distributions).
Evaluation breadth is somewhat limited to COCO in the main results, with ResNet-50 students only in the main table; VOC/BDD100K results are single-run and relegated to the appendix.

Presentation: Figure 2 is dense and hard to parse; the score-threshold-domain derivation requires careful reading, and several design choices (fixed T:F = 1:9, 6th-order polynomial surrogates) are stated pragmatically rather than justified theoretically.

strengths: The core technical contribution is well developed: the derivation of a closed-form estimator for the marginal effect of a single TP/FP insertion on dataset-level AP (Eqs. 6-10, full derivation in Appendix A3) is clean, and the Monte Carlo verification in Appendix 4 convincingly validates the analytic forms against direct simulation (agreement within ~1e-4).

The evaluation is unusually comprehensive for this topic: six detector families (Faster R-CNN, ATSS, FCOS, GFL, VFNet, Deformable DETR), ablations on teacher capacity, prior choice, augmentation interaction, noise robustness (Fig. 5), pseudo-labeling (Appendix 2), additional datasets (VOC, BDD100K), and long-schedule behavior (Table 13).

The paper is candid about limitations, including the extra teacher forward pass, the approximate nature of the first-order additivity assumption (Appendix A3.4 quantifies it), and the fact that the uniform prior trades accuracy for generality (Appendix 6 shows the model-specific prior helps training but not validation).

The comparison in Table 4 is informative: DetGain is contrasted against uniform, GradNorm, hard mining, entropy, and the Image-AP metric of Zhou et al. [62] under the same online batch-selection protocol, showing consistent gains (~+1.1-1.7 AP over the closest baseline).

The combination with strong online augmentation (Sec. 3.3, Table 2) is a sensible fix for the overfitting that pure learnability-based subsampling causes, and the ablation clearly isolates the two effects.
weaknesses: The computational cost substantially undercuts the paper's 'data-efficient learning' framing. Table 12 reports a ~200% wall-clock overhead per iteration: each iteration requires teacher and student forward passes over the full 80-image super-batch (with strong augmentation) to backprop on only 16 images. Figure 9's claim of reaching baseline performance in 52% of iterations does not account for the ~3x per-iteration cost, so wall-clock efficiency gains appear marginal at best. The dynamic ratio schedule partially mitigates this, but the headline efficiency story is overstated.

The method depends on a pretrained teacher trained on the same data with a larger backbone, which confounds the claimed gains with implicit knowledge distillation through data selection. Table 3 shows gains scale with teacher capacity (37.4 -> 40.9/39.9/40.0 with Res50/Res101/Res152 teachers), and Appendix 1 shows cross-family teachers degrade results. While Sec. 4.5 compares to PKD/CrossKD, the paper does not fully disentangle whether DetGain is competitive with simply distilling, given its 3x training cost.

Absolute gains on clean COCO are modest (~+2 mAP average), and the improvement over the closest prior online metric (Image-AP [62], which the method essentially extends from offline to online) is only ~+1 AP. The novelty over [62] is thus incremental: primarily the online setting, the closed-form marginal estimator, and the augmentation coupling.

The uniform-prior simplification (f_TP = f_FP = 1) with a fixed T:F = 1:9 ratio, while pragmatic, means the 'marginal contribution to mAP' signal actually used for selection is quite far from the quantity defined in Eq. 2; the paper's framing as metric-aligned scoring is stronger than what the deployed surrogate delivers, even if ranking agreement is empirically high.

Scalability of the scoring to stronger augmentation and other pipelines is asserted but the augmentation probabilities are 'adjusted per model family' by hand (Appendix 5, Table 9), introducing per-detector tuning that sits uneasily with the claimed model-agnostic, plug-and-play nature.

Some key implementation choices affecting reproducibility (exact augmentation branch probabilities per detector, the polynomial surrogate fitting in the supplementary, teacher training schedules) are scattered across the appendix, and no code release is mentioned.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: online data selection for object detection is genuinely underexplored relative to classification/multimodal curation, and the paper identifies concrete technical reasons (multi-task, fragmented losses, proposal assignment dynamics) why generic learnability signals fail.

The core technical idea is original and non-trivial: reformulating learnability as the marginal perturbation of dataset-level mAP from a single image, and deriving closed-form single-insertion ΔAP expressions for TP/FP insertion (Eqs. 7-8, 10) from the precision-recall/Sieltjes formulation of AP. The derivation in Appendix A3 is complete and the Monte Carlo verification (Appendix 4, Fig. 7) plus additivity/ranking-stability analysis (Fig. 6) provide unusually careful empirical validation of the approximation.

Comprehensive and mostly rigorous evaluation: six representative detectors spanning one-stage, two-stage, and transformer families (Table 1), comparison against a broad set of alternative sampling metrics under a unified protocol (Table 4), ablations on teacher capacity, prior choice, augmentation interplay (Table 2), long-schedule behavior (Table 13), noisy annotations (Fig. 5), pseudo-labels (Table 7), and additional datasets (VOC, BDD100K). Main results are reported as mean±std over three seeds.

The combination of strong online augmentation with score-based subsampling (Sec. 3.3) is a sensible and empirically supported remedy for the overfitting of pure selective sampling, and the complementarity analysis with KD methods (Table 5, Sec. 4.5) situates the contribution well relative to prior art.

Honest limitations section: added pre-scanning time and naive augmentation pipeline are acknowledged. Runtime/memory accounting is transparently reported (Table 12), and the convergence-speed result (Fig. 9, similar performance in ~52% of iterations) is a practically relevant claim.
weaknesses: Substantial training overhead: per-iteration time grows from 0.25s to 0.75s (+200%) for Faster R-CNN at k=20% (Table 12). The paper frames the method as data-efficient, but the net wall-clock benefit is not clearly established: a 48-52% iteration saving (Fig. 9) is likely offset or outweighed by the ~3x per-iteration cost. A wall-clock-matched comparison against the baseline would considerably strengthen the practical claims.

Conceptual novelty relative to prior work is incremental in part: the teacher-student learnability-gap sampling recipe is inherited from RHO-LOSS/ACED, and the contribution is primarily the replacement of the loss gap with a dataset-level AP-based score. The paper does argue this distinction well, but the framing as 'the first data-efficient online curation pipeline' (Sec. 5) overstates it.

Several heuristic simplifications are only partially justified: the universal uniform prior for TP/FP score distributions, the fixed global T:F = 1:9 ratio (Appendix A3.3), and per-detector-family augmentation probabilities (Table 9, 'adjustments observed empirically'). The last point raises a mild concern about tuning effort applied to the proposed pipeline that the baselines may not receive, although Table 4 does use a unified protocol.

The mechanism behind augmentation+subsampling generalization (Sec. 3.3, Table 2) is described intuitively (expanded data space) but not analyzed quantitatively; the observed training-AP inflation (50.3 train vs 37.3 val under sampling alone) deserves deeper analysis.

First-order additivity (Eq. 27) and the single-image insertion analysis ignore interactions among detections within a selected sub-batch; validation is simulation-based on fitted detector outputs, and a direct empirical check on real training runs (e.g., correlation between predicted batch gains and realized mAP gains over time) is absent.

Some results are single-run (Table 11, Table 10), and gains on smaller datasets (VOC +3.0, BDD100K +1.8) have wider unquantified variance. Missing-codebase details for baselines are mostly handled by following MMDetection defaults, but reproducibility depends on the promised released pipeline.
